**Source.** The examples on this page are transcribed from the PianoGroove handout
*Walking Bass Line Theory: Lesson Notation & Graphics*
([www.pianogroove.com](https://www.pianogroove.com)), from its lesson on organ walking bass.

A **walking bass line** moves one note to every beat, four to the bar, and keeps going
from chord to chord. The organist plays it with the left hand (or the pedals) while the
right hand comps or solos. All five lines here are over a blues in F, written in the bass
clef, and swung.

**How to read the examples.** Notes marked **gh** are *ghost notes*: in the handout they
are printed in brackets. A ghost note is barely played: touched, felt more than heard,
so the eighth before it sounds like a little push into the next beat. Each ▶ plays the
line with the band (the band's own bass player sits out, so the line you hear is the one
written; it is played on the band's piano). "▶ Chords" plays only the chords.

## 1. Ghost-note approaches

The whole 12-bar blues, walking almost all the way in quarter notes. Three things decorate
it. At the end of bars 1, 6 and 9 the last beat is split into two eighths: B♮ then a
ghost B♭ (bar 6 starts with F and a ghost F). The B♮ is a half step *below* C, the note
the next bar wants, so the ghost just fills the beat. Bars 3 and 10 open with a quick
eighth-note **triplet** down the chord (F C A, then C G E) before landing on the root an
octave lower. Bar 8 ends with a triplet D A A♭ that slides down a half step into G for
the Gm7 of bar 9.

"Bb7"_B,,2 D,2 _E,2 =E,2 | F,"^gh"F, A,,2 _B,,2 =B,,"^gh"_B,, | "F7"C,2 C,2 _B,,2 _B,,2 | "Am7b5"A,,2 _E,"^gh"A,, "D7"D,2 (3D,A,,_A,, |
"Gm7"G,,2 A,,2 _B,,2 =B,,"^gh"_B,, | "C7"(3C,G,,E,, C,,2 D,,2 E,,"^gh"D,, | "F7"F,,4 z4 | z8 |]

## 2. Chromatic approach

Only the first five bars are written out (the handout leaves the rest as slashes for you
to fill in; the band keeps the chords going). Listen for half steps. In bar 1, F G A♭ A
climbs chromatically from G into B♭, the root of the next bar. Bar 2 does the same thing
higher up: E♭ E♮ leads into F. In bar 3, D D♭ slides down into C for the Cm7. In bar 4,
C G♭ F walks *down* by half step onto the F of F7, then B♮ is a half step below the B♭
of bar 5.

<script type="text/plain">

M:4/4
L:1/8

K:F clef=bass

"Bb7"_B,,2 z6 | z8 | "F7"z8 | "Am7b5"z4 "D7"z4 |]

## 3. Scalar approach

Here the line runs down and up the scale that goes with each chord. Bar 1 walks straight
down from F: F E♭ D C (the F7 chord's scale has E♭, not E). Bar 2 does the same from
B♭: B♭ A♭ G, then G♭ a half step above F. Bar 3 climbs F A B♭ B♮ into C, and bar 4 C G A♭
B♮ ends with the same half step into B♭.

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="132" data-style="swing" data-bass="off" data-width="640">
<script type="text/plain">
T:Example 3: with scalar approach
M:4/4
L:1/8
Q:1/4=132
K:F clef=bass
"F7"F,2 _E,2 D,2 C,2 | "Bb7"_B,,2 _A,,2 G,,2 _G,,2 | "F7"F,,2 A,,2 _B,,2 =B,,2 | "Cm7"C,2 G,,2 "F7"_A,,2 =B,,2 |
"Bb7"_B,,2 z6 | z8 | "F7"z8 | "Am7b5"z4 "D7"z4 |]
</script>
</div>

## 4. Interval jump approach

Bars 1 and 2 are the scale runs of example 3. The new idea is the **leap**: in bar 3 the
line climbs F G A and then jumps up a fourth to D, which leads down a step to the C of
bar 4. In bar 4 it jumps the other way, from C down a sixth to E♭, then climbs by half steps,
E♭ E♮ F, so beat 4 is the root of the F7, a fourth below the B♭ of bar 5. A jump
changes register quickly, which is useful when the line is about to run out of room.
Bar 5 brings back the B♭ D E♭ E♮ of example 2.

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="132" data-style="swing" data-bass="off" data-width="640">
<script type="text/plain">
T:Example 4: interval jump approach
M:4/4
L:1/8
Q:1/4=132
K:F clef=bass
"F7"F,2 _E,2 D,2 C,2 | "Bb7"_B,,2 _A,,2 G,,2 _G,,2 | "F7"F,,2 G,,2 A,,2 D,2 | "Cm7"C,2 _E,,2 "F7"=E,,2 F,,2 |
"Bb7"_B,,2 D,2 _E,2 =E,2 | F,2 z6 | "F7"z8 | "Am7b5"z4 "D7"z4 |]
</script>
</div>

## 5. Enclosures

An **enclosure** surrounds a target note: one note above it and one below (or the other
way round) before landing on it, the way a right-hand bebop line does. Bar 2 ends C, then
G♭ a half step above F, and the line drops to the F of bar 3. Bar 4's G♭ F B♮ and bar 7's B♭ A♭ (around A of bar 8) work the same way.
Bar 8 is A E♭ D A♭: D7 is reached, then A♭ a half step above G for Gm7. Bar 9 is the busiest
bar: G, then A B♭ D♭ each followed by a ghost G, so the line climbs while the G keeps
sounding underneath like a pedal. D♭ is a half step above C, the root of bar 10.

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="132" data-style="swing" data-bass="off" data-width="640">
<script type="text/plain">
T:Example 5: with enclosures
M:4/4
L:1/8
Q:1/4=132
K:F clef=bass
"F7"F,,2 A,,2 _B,,2 =B,,2 | C,2 D,2 C,2 _G,,2 | F,,2 A,,2 _B,,2 =B,,2 | "Cm7"C,2 _G,,2 "F7"F,,2 =B,,2 |
"Bb7"_B,,2 D,2 _E,2 =E,2 | F,2 A,,2 _B,,2 =B,,2 | "F7"C,2 A,,2 _B,,2 _A,,2 | "Am7b5"A,,2 _E,,2 "D7"D,,2 _A,,2 |
"Gm7"G,,2 A,,"^gh"G,, _B,,"^gh"G,, _D,"^gh"G,, | "C7"C,2 _B,,2 _G,,2 E,,2 | "F7"F,,2 A,,2 _B,,2 =B,,2 | C,2 z6 |]
</script>
</div>

## Practice tips

These are the handout's suggestions, in our words.

- **Aim at chord tones.** Find the root (or 3rd, or 5th) the next bar wants and get there
  from a half step above or below on beat 4.
- **Know the scale of each chord.** A scale that fits the chord gives you notes that walk
  smoothly; run up or down it between chord tones.
- **Borrow enclosures from the right hand.** The above-and-below patterns of bebop
  melody lines work just as well in the left hand.
- **Study and transcribe.** Learn these five lines, then write out what jazz organists
  play. The handout names Richard "Groove" Holmes, Jimmy Smith, Jimmy McGriff, Jack McDuff,
  Charles Earland and Shirley Scott, and, more recently, Tony Monaco, Larry Goldings,
  Joey DeFrancesco, Pat Bianchi, Mike LeDonne, Jared Gold and Brian Charette.
